To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the stereotype vulnerability of African-American test takers impairs their intellectual test performance.

African American students underperformed relative to European American students on a verbal test when their scores were made diagnostic of their ability, but not when their scores were not diagnostic of their ability.
the performance of African Americans on a verbal ability test can be impaired by their awareness of the negative stereotype about their group's intellectual ability.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the impact on the intellectual test performance by African Americans of the risk of confirming, in the eyes of others, a negative stereotype concerning their intellectual abilities.
the impact of social identity threat on the intellectual test performance, and more generally, the intellectual functioning of stigmatized group members.
how the threat of confirming a stereotype about one's social group can undermine intellectual performance.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the stereotype threat is a psychological phenomenon that is a threat to the intellectual performance of the African Americans.
stereotype threat has been found to impair intellectual performance of the African Americans, but not the Asian Americans.
stereotype threat is a significant factor in the standardized test scores of African Americans.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
stereotype vulnerability can be an impediment to performance for members of stigmatized groups.
when a test is diagnostic of ability, African Americans underperform because they are concerned about confirming a negative stereotype about their intellectual abilities.

the stereotype vulnerability of African Americans can impair their performance in intellectual domains in which the stereotype is applicable, and that this vulnerability can be reduced by eliminating diagnosticity of the test or by eliminating the salience of the negative stereotype about their group. The main takeaway from our work is that
the mere salience of negative stereotypes about one's group can have a negative effect on one's performance on a test that is not ability diagnostic.
stereotype threat is not simply a cognitive bias that can be overcome by cognitive strategies.

the stereotype threat effect is not limited to the domain of intellectual ability, but rather, it can occur in any domain in which a person is at risk of confirming a negative stereotype about his/her group (e.g., the stereotype that Blacks have low math ability, that older adults have poor memory, or that women have poor mechanical skills).
